title: The neighbour who remembers me
subtitle: A greeting becomes a small invitation.
ending: I leave with a name, a wave, and something to say next time. The courtyard is the same size. Somehow it feels less anonymous.

scenes.title: Someone knows my face
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: I step into the courtyard before school. My bag catches the door, which makes a much louder entrance than I intended.
A woman with a canvas shopping bag smiles. This is Ms Lin, the neighbour I have nodded to all week. Today she waits for more than a nod. I want to introduce myself before I have to leave.

line.pinyin: nǐ hǎo ！ nǐ zhù zhè lǐ ma ？

choices.label: Say that I live here
choices.response: Ms Lin points upstairs, then at herself. Two people in one building have finally become neighbours.
choices.hint: Put the person first, then what they do. Keep the question particle at the end.

choices.label: Return her greeting
choices.response: She shifts the shopping bag to shake my hand. We are officially past the nodding stage.
choices.hint: Keep the greeting first; 很高兴 belongs before 认识你.

aside.question: Look at her shopping bag
aside.answer: A spring onion sticks out like a green flag. She notices me looking and tucks it back in. It immediately escapes again.

scenes.title: A name to remember
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: Ms Lin introduces herself slowly. I repeat her surname once, and she nods.
A scooter rolls past. For a moment I consider letting its engine do all the talking. Instead, I offer my name.

line.english: My surname is Lin. What is your name?
line.pinyin: wǒ xìng lín 。 nǐ jiào shén me míng zì ？

choices.label: Introduce myself as David
choices.response: “David,” she repeats carefully. She gives my name the same attention I gave hers.
choices.hint: 叫 comes between 我 and the name.

aside.question: Ask how to address her
aside.answer: Ms Lin gestures to herself and repeats her surname. “Ms Lin” is a comfortable name for this fictional neighbour; I do not need a complicated title to begin.

scenes.title: The books give me away
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: She notices the books in my bag and points toward the school gate.
I want to explain my work, not deliver my entire employment history beside a bicycle rack. One clear sentence will do.

line.pinyin: nǐ shì lǎo shī ma ？

choices.label: Explain that I teach English
choices.response: Ms Lin grins and mimes a classroom full of raised hands. I mime a very large cup of coffee. We both understand.
choices.hint: Use 我 + 是 + the occupation.

aside.question: Notice what she remembers
aside.answer: She remembers seeing me carry books yesterday. It is a small kindness: someone has been paying attention.

scenes.title: One sentence too fast
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: Her next question comes with a smile, a gesture, and more syllables than I can comfortably hold.
I catch “Chinese.” The rest has already left the station. I could nod, but then I would have agreed to something I do not understand.

line.pinyin: nǐ zài xué zhōng wén ma ？

choices.label: Ask her to say it again
choices.response: She repeats the question slowly, without making a performance of my difficulty. This is a conversation, not an exam.
choices.hint: 再 goes before 说; 一遍 tells how many repetitions.

rich.english: Could you please say it again?

choices.label: Ask her to speak a little slowly

simple.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

choices.response: She slows down. The words separate themselves into something I can answer.
choices.hint: 慢一点 describes how to speak, so it follows 说.

rich.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

aside.question: Recall what I heard
aside.answer: She is asking whether I am learning Chinese. Asking for repetition keeps the conversation alive; it does not mean I have failed.

scenes.title: A small honest answer
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: This time I hear the question. Ms Lin waits, balancing her bag on the bicycle seat.
I can say a little. That is different from saying nothing.

line.pinyin: nǐ huì shuō zhōng wén ma ？

choices.label: Say that I speak a little

simple.english: I can speak a little Chinese.

choices.response: She holds her fingers a little apart, then opens her hand wider: a little can grow.
choices.hint: 一点 belongs before 中文 here.

rich.english: I can speak a little Chinese.

choices.label: Say that I am learning
choices.response: She nods toward herself as if volunteering to be part of the practice.
choices.hint: 在学 means “am learning.”

aside.question: Ask about her morning
aside.answer: She points to her shopping bag, then the teahouse. Shopping first, tea later. Her morning has a sensible order.

scenes.title: Ask something back
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: The clock above the gate reminds me that I still have a job to get to. But I do not want to disappear immediately after talking about myself.
Across the courtyard, a woman is setting cups on a table. Ms Lin waves to her. I can ask about the place or about her plans.

line.english: You can drink tea over there.
line.pinyin: nà biān kě yǐ hē chá 。

choices.label: Ask whether she likes tea
choices.response: She laughs and points at her cup-shaped hand. That appears to be a very enthusiastic yes.
choices.hint: Keep 吗 at the end.

choices.label: Ask if she is free on the weekend

simple.english: Are you free on the weekend?

choices.response: She considers, then points to Saturday on her phone. There may be a conversation with more time in it.
choices.hint: Put 周末 before 有空.

rich.english: Are you free on the weekend?

aside.question: Look toward the teahouse
aside.answer: The owner catches our wave. Ms Lin calls her Ms Zhou. I have not met her yet, but I now have another face to recognise.

scenes.title: An invitation, not a test
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: Ms Lin offers to meet for tea on Saturday. I check the time: I can still reach school without running.
I can accept, or leave the invitation for another day. Either way, I want to answer warmly and clearly.

line.english: Shall we have tea together on Saturday?
line.pinyin: xīng qī liù yī qǐ hē chá ， hǎo ma ？

choices.label: Accept the invitation
choices.response: She taps Saturday on her phone and waves me toward school. I walk away with an actual plan.
choices.hint: We comes before the meeting time in this version.

choices.label: Thank her and suggest another day

simple.english: Thank you; let’s have tea another day.

choices.response: She nods, with no sign of offence. An invitation can stay open without becoming a promise.
choices.hint: 改天 means another day; put it before 喝茶.

rich.english: Thank you; let’s have tea another day.

aside.question: Remember the first greeting
aside.answer: This morning began with a nod. Now I can introduce myself, explain my work, and ask for help when a sentence is too fast.

title: A weekend plan, almost
subtitle: Find a shared interest. Agree on the same day.
ending: I put the meeting in my calendar. The plan is modest: a conversation and a cup of tea. It is also clear, which feels like a useful kind of victory.

scenes.title: The kettle conference
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: At school, I reach the kettle at the same time as Chen, a colleague with round glasses and a stack of exercise books.
We have exchanged plenty of “hello”s. Today he asks a question that could turn into a real conversation. I want to find something we both enjoy.

line.pinyin: nǐ zhōu mò yǒu kōng ma ？

choices.label: Say that I am free on Saturday
choices.response: Chen puts down the books. A possible plan has his attention.
choices.hint: Put the time before 有空.

choices.label: Ask about his weekend first

simple.english: What do you do on the weekend?

choices.response: He points to a book, then draws a cup in the air. We may have found common ground.
choices.hint: Put 周末 between 你 and 做什么.

rich.english: What do you do on the weekend?

aside.question: Ask about the stack of books
aside.answer: Chen balances them with the expertise of someone who has tried carrying one too many. We both quietly move our tea farther from the edge.

callback.text: I remember accepting Ms Lin’s invitation. Perhaps I can introduce two people instead of trying to hold two separate plans.

scenes.title: Something in common
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: Chen tells me he likes books and tea. I can answer about either.
I do not need to invent an impressive hobby. A genuine small interest gives us somewhere to begin.

line.pinyin: nǐ xǐ huan zuò shén me ？

choices.label: Talk about reading
choices.response: He points to the least battered book in his stack and tells me it is his own. That explains the careful balancing.
choices.hint: 喜欢 comes before the activity.

choices.label: Talk about tea
choices.response: He lifts his mug. There is already evidence for this shared interest.
choices.hint: 喜欢 comes before the activity.

aside.question: Keep the conversation going
aside.answer: A shared interest need not be a grand passion. “I like tea” can be enough to suggest doing something together.

scenes.title: Make the invitation
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: The kettle clicks off. Chen has not reached for his books yet.
I think of the courtyard teahouse: close enough to describe, quiet enough to practise a conversation. I decide to invite him.

line.pinyin: wǒ men qù nǎ lǐ ？

choices.label: Suggest going for tea together
choices.response: Chen agrees. Now there are two people imagining the same sort of afternoon.
choices.hint: 吧 softens a suggestion; keep it at the end.

aside.question: Describe the teahouse simply
aside.answer: I can point to its location on a map when we finish. Knowing the exact address matters more than pretending I can already explain every turn.

scenes.title: Two calendars, two days
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: Chen says a day and types it into his phone. I glance at the screen: Sunday.
I meant Saturday. If I only smile now, one of us will be drinking a very lonely cup of tea. I need to correct the day without making the mix-up a big event.

line.pinyin: xīng qī tiān ， duì ma ？

choices.label: Clarify: Saturday, not Sunday
choices.response: He checks the screen, laughs, and changes the day. We have caught the problem while it is still small.
choices.hint: Use 是 X, 不是 Y to contrast the two days.

aside.question: Compare the two day names
aside.answer: 星期六 means Saturday. 星期天 means Sunday. I listen for the last part rather than treating the whole phrase as one long blur.

scenes.title: A time we can keep
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: Chen draws a little sun above the corrected date. Afternoon works better for him.
I can suggest two or three. Both are real options; the useful part is making one clear.

line.pinyin: xià wǔ jǐ diǎn ？

choices.label: Suggest two in the afternoon

simple.english: Let’s meet at two in the afternoon.

choices.response: He enters two o’clock. I enter it too. Matching calendars are a surprisingly satisfying sight.
choices.hint: The time goes before 见.

rich.english: Let’s meet at two in the afternoon.

choices.label: Suggest three in the afternoon

simple.english: Let’s meet at three in the afternoon.

choices.response: He enters three o’clock. There is time for lunch first, and nobody has to guess.
choices.hint: The time goes before 见.

rich.english: Let’s meet at three in the afternoon.

aside.question: Check the map together
aside.answer: I show him the teahouse near my courtyard. He saves the pin. We have a place as well as a day and a time.

scenes.title: Someone else might come
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: I mention a neighbour who knows the teahouse owner. Chen asks whether she will be there too.
I can suggest inviting her, or explain that I do not know yet. I should not promise someone else’s afternoon for them.

line.pinyin: nǐ de péng yǒu yě lái ma ？

choices.label: Suggest asking her
choices.response: Chen nods. Asking leaves Ms Lin free to decide for herself.
choices.hint: 可以 goes before 问问.

choices.label: Say that I do not know yet
choices.response: That answer turns out to be enough. Chen has no objection to a plan with one detail still open.
choices.hint: 还 belongs before 不知道.

aside.question: Remember Ms Lin’s invitation
aside.answer: Whether I accepted or postponed it, the conversation gave me a way to ask again. A polite answer need not close a door.

scenes.title: Say it once more
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: The bell interrupts us. Chen collects his books, and I reach for my mug.
Before we leave, I want to confirm the day we corrected. Saying it once more now is easier than explaining an empty table later.

line.pinyin: hǎo ， zhōu mò jiàn ！

choices.label: Confirm Saturday before leaving
choices.response: Chen points at the corrected calendar entry. We both laugh about Sunday, which is now free to remain Sunday.
choices.hint: Put the meeting time before 见.

aside.question: Recall what changed
aside.answer: I found a shared interest, suggested an activity, and corrected a misunderstanding. The correction helped the conversation rather than spoiling it.

title: One more cup
subtitle: Introduce two people. Let the afternoon change.
ending: Rain taps the roof while I finish my tea. I have introduced people, asked questions, and changed a plan. My Chinese is still small. The afternoon has made room for it.

scenes.title: The right table
scenes.speaker: zhou
paragraphs: I step into the neighbourhood teahouse. Ms Zhou, the owner, catches a cup before it rolls off a tray. She looks pleased that I have not arrived during the catching part.
Chen is nearby, looking for a table. Ms Lin is already here after shopping. Whether invited or simply passing through, she has found the best chair.

line.english: Hello! Please sit. What tea would you like?
line.pinyin: nǐ hǎo ！ qǐng zuò 。 hē shén me chá ？

choices.label: Ask for hot tea
choices.response: Ms Zhou sets out a warm cup. Steam curls upward while I take off my bag.
choices.hint: 想喝 goes before the drink.

rich.english: I would like a cup of hot tea.

choices.label: Ask for water first

simple.english: Please give me a glass of water.

choices.response: Water arrives without fuss. I have time to settle in before choosing tea.
choices.hint: 请 softens the request; the drink follows 给我.

rich.english: Please give me a glass of water.

aside.question: Notice the room
aside.answer: Bamboo chairs scrape gently across the floor. Nobody seems in a hurry to make a cup of tea into a schedule.

callback.text: My phone shows the three-o’clock meeting I arranged with Chen. This time our calendars and our feet agree.

scenes.title: Put two names together
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: Ms Lin waves Chen toward our table. He looks at me, waiting for an introduction.
I know who everyone is. They do not. This is a small piece of useful Chinese I can supply.

line.pinyin: zhè shì shuí ？

choices.label: Introduce Chen as my colleague
choices.response: Chen introduces himself. Ms Lin makes room for his chair, and I no longer have to carry both sides of the conversation.
choices.hint: 我的 describes 同事; keep those together.

rich.english: This is my colleague; his surname is Chen.

aside.question: Introduce Ms Lin too
aside.answer: I gesture toward Ms Lin and say her name. Chen greets her. Names and a welcoming gesture do some of the work while I learn the longer sentence.

scenes.title: The question comes back
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: Chen asks Ms Lin about the book beside her cup. She tells him it belongs to the owner.
The question turns back toward me. I can ask Chen about reading, or include Ms Lin by asking about tea.

line.english: What would you like to talk about?
line.pinyin: nǐ xiǎng liáo shén me ？

choices.label: Ask Chen about reading
choices.response: Chen leans forward. He describes a book in short sentences, checking that I can follow.
choices.hint: Put 吗 at the end.

choices.label: Ask Ms Lin about tea
choices.response: Ms Lin lifts her cup with a theatrical seriousness. Even before the answer, I understand her position.
choices.hint: Put 吗 at the end.

aside.question: Ask a follow-up about the book
aside.answer: Chen shows me the cover rather than reciting a complicated summary. I can ask someone to show me something as well as explain it.

callback.text: I remember telling Chen that I like reading. He has brought a book to show me; our last conversation has travelled with him.

scenes.title: One detail about my life
scenes.speaker: lin
paragraphs: Ms Lin points to Chen’s book and remembers the books in my bag outside the courtyard.
She asks about school. I can explain what I teach or where I work. There is no need to list every class.

line.pinyin: nǐ jiào shén me ？

choices.label: Say that I teach English
choices.response: Chen nods, then slowly tells Ms Lin that we work together. A familiar fact becomes a conversation among three people.
choices.hint: 教 is the verb; 英语 is what I teach.

choices.label: Explain that I am a teacher
choices.response: Ms Lin remembers the courtyard conversation. This time I say the sentence without searching quite so hard.
choices.hint: 是 links 我 with the occupation.

aside.question: Notice the callback
aside.answer: I have used the same idea in two places now. The person listening has changed; the sentence still works.

scenes.title: A word under the rain
scenes.speaker: zhou
paragraphs: A sudden pattering begins on the roof. Ms Zhou looks outside and says something while moving a chair away from the doorway.
I hear the first words, then rain swallows the rest. This is exactly what a request for repetition is for.

line.english: It is raining. Wait a little before leaving.
line.pinyin: xià yǔ le 。 děng yí xià zài zǒu ba 。

choices.label: Ask Ms Zhou to repeat that
choices.response: She points to the rain, then the dry chairs, and repeats herself. The room supplies clues as well as words.
choices.hint: 再 goes before 说; 一遍 finishes the request.

choices.label: Ask her to speak more slowly

simple.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

choices.response: She repeats it more slowly. I catch both the weather and her practical suggestion.
choices.hint: 慢一点 follows 说.

rich.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

aside.question: Look outside
aside.answer: The courtyard stones are darkening. Waiting here would be comfortable; leaving would mean finding an umbrella.

scenes.title: Change the plan
scenes.speaker: chen
paragraphs: Chen looks at the rain, then at the nearly empty teapot. We had thought about a walk. The weather has another suggestion.
I can propose waiting here or asking for an umbrella. Both keep the afternoon moving, in different ways.

line.pinyin: wǒ men xiàn zài zǒu ma ？

choices.label: Suggest waiting here a little
choices.response: Ms Zhou refills the pot. The walk becomes a longer conversation, which was most of the point anyway.
choices.hint: Place 在这里 before 等一下.

choices.label: Suggest borrowing an umbrella

simple.english: Let’s borrow an umbrella before leaving.

choices.response: Ms Zhou points to a spare umbrella. We agree to return it; the next visit now has a small purpose.
choices.hint: 再走 comes after borrowing the umbrella.

rich.english: Let’s borrow an umbrella before leaving.

aside.question: Consider what matters
aside.answer: The afternoon does not need to follow the original plan to go well. I need language for changing it together.

scenes.title: Leave the next conversation open
scenes.speaker: zhou
paragraphs: Eventually the rain softens. I have my bag, Chen has his book, and Ms Lin has somehow acquired another spring onion.
I want to thank Ms Zhou and leave warmly. I do not need a perfect final speech. I need something I can say again next time.

line.pinyin: xià cì zài lái ！

choices.label: Thank her and say goodbye

simple.english: Thank you; see you next time.

choices.response: Ms Zhou waves from the doorway. The next greeting already feels a little easier.
choices.hint: 下次 sets the time for 再见.

rich.english: Thank you; see you next time.

choices.label: Suggest tea together again

simple.english: Let’s have tea together next time.

choices.response: Ms Lin raises one finger as if putting it straight into her calendar. Chen laughs and checks which day she means.
choices.hint: Keep 吧 at the end of the suggestion.

rich.english: Let’s have tea together next time.

aside.question: Recall the afternoon
aside.answer: I introduced a colleague, asked about an interest, explained my work, and asked for repetition. Familiar pieces made a new conversation.
